[2024 summer phd probability — problem 4]

Part II. Let $(V, E)$ be a finite undirected graph, $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$, with $v \sim v'$ iff $\{v, v'\} \in E$. State space $\mathcal{X} = \{-1, 1\}^n$ (spin configurations). Define $H(x) = \sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}\mathbb{1}\{x(v) \ne x(v')\} = \tfrac12\sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}(1 - x(v)x(v'))$ and $\pi(x) = \frac{e^{-H(x)}}{\sum_y e^{-H(y)}}$. The update $X_{t+1} = f_{t+1}(x_t)$: sample $v_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}(V)$, $S_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{-1,1\}$, $U_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$; propose $y$ with $y(v_{t+1}) = S_{t+1}$, $y(w) = x_t(w)$ otherwise; accept ($f_{t+1}(x_t) = y$) if $U_{t+1} \le \min\{1, e^{-H(y)}/e^{-H(x_t)}\}$, else reject. $P(x, z) = P(f_{t+1}(x) = z)$.
(1) Compute $P(x, z)$ for $z \ne x$ with $P(x, z) > 0$ (need not compute $P(x, x)$).
(2) Prove $\pi$ is stationary for this chain.
(3) With $N_{t+1} \subset V$ the neighbors of $v_{t+1}$ and $y$ the proposed move, show $\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}} = \exp(\tfrac12\sum_{w \in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1} - x_t(v_{t+1})) x_t(w))$.
(4) Write $x \preceq y$ if $x(v) \le y(v)$ for all $v$. Prove that if $x \preceq z$ then $P(f_{t+1}(x) \preceq f_{t+1}(z)) = 1$ (handle $S_{t+1} = \pm1$ separately) — i.e. the dynamics is monotone.
(5) Let $\underline x = (-1, \dots, -1)$, $\bar x = (1, \dots, 1)$. Prove $F = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ is constant iff $F(\underline x) = F(\bar x)$. Let $T = \min\{t \ge 1 : f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x) = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)\}$.
(6) For $z \in \mathcal{X}$, let $h(z)$ be the max number $k$ of distinct states $x_1 \preceq \cdots \preceq x_k = z$. Prove that if $x_t \preceq y_t$ and $x_t \ne y_t$ then $h(x_t) + 1 \le h(y_t)$.
(7) With $X_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x)$, $Y_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)$ (so $\{T > t\} = \{X_t \ne Y_t\}$), prove $P(T > t) \le \mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)]$.
(8) Prove $0 \le h(z) \le |V|$ and $\mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)] \le |V|\,\bar d(t)$.
(9) If $|V| = 2L$ ($L > 1$ integer) and $k \ge 0$, prove $P(T > t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k + L)) \le \frac{1}{2^k}$ (state the properties of $d, \bar d, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ used).
(10) Prove $\mathbb{E}[T] \le c\, L\, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ for an absolute constant $c > 0$ (you may first show any nonnegative $U$ with $P(U > k) \le 1/2^k$ for all integers $k \ge 0$ has finite expectation).

Let \(n=|V|\), and write \(x_v=x(v)\). Also write  
\[
D(x,z):=\{v\in V:x_v\neq z_v\}.
\]

---

## (1) Off-diagonal transition probabilities

If \(z\neq x\), then \(P(x,z)>0\) only if \(z\) differs from \(x\) at exactly one vertex. Suppose \(D(x,z)=\{v\}\). Then the proposal \(z\) is made exactly when \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z_v\), which has probability \(\frac1n\cdot \frac12=\frac1{2n}\). Hence

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]

Thus, for \(z\neq x\),

\[
\boxed{
P(x,z)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}, & |D(x,z)|=1,\\[1.2ex]
0, & |D(x,z)|\ge 2.
\end{cases}}
\]

Equivalently, if \(D(x,z)=\{v\}\),

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\exp\left(\frac12(z_v-x_v)\sum_{w\sim v}x_w\right)\right\}.
\]

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

Let \(Z=\sum_y e^{-H(y)}\), so \(\pi(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-H(x)}\).

We prove detailed balance. If \(x,z\) differ at more than one coordinate, then \(P(x,z)=P(z,x)=0\). If \(x,z\) differ at exactly one coordinate, then by part (1),

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

Thus

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]

The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\), so

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

The equality is trivial for \(x=z\). Hence the chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). Therefore, by the detailed balance theorem,

\[
\sum_x \pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\sum_x \pi(z)P(z,x)
=
\pi(z)\sum_x P(z,x)
=
\pi(z).
\]

So \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local expression for the acceptance ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and let \(N_v=\{w:w\sim v\}\). The proposed configuration \(y\) differs from \(x_t\) only at \(v\), with \(y_v=S\). Therefore all non-incident edges cancel in \(H(y)-H(x_t)\). Thus

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}
\Big[(1-Sx_t(w))-(1-x_t(v)x_t(w))\Big].
\]

Simplifying,

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(x_t(v)-S)x_t(w).
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
e^{-(H(y)-H(x_t))}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(S-x_t(v))x_t(w)
\right).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1}-x_t(v_{t+1}))x_t(w)\right).
}
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

Fix a realization of \((v_{t+1},S_{t+1},U_{t+1})\). We show that if \(x\preceq z\), then

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

For coordinates \(w\neq v_{t+1}\), neither update changes the spin, so

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_w=x_w\le z_w=f_{t+1}(z)_w.
\]

Thus we only need to check the chosen vertex \(v=v_{t+1}\).

Let

\[
\Sigma_\eta:=\sum_{w\sim v}\eta_w
\]

for a configuration \(\eta\).

### Case 1: \(S_{t+1}=+1\)

If \(z_v=+1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)_v=+1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le +1=f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(z_v=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(x_v=-1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(-1\) to \(+1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
a(x)\le a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the lower chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(x)\), then necessarily \(U\le a(z)\), so the upper chain also accepts. Hence the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur. Therefore

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

### Case 2: \(S_{t+1}=-1\)

If \(x_v=-1\), then \(f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(x_v=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(z_v=+1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(+1\) to \(-1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
e^{-\Sigma_x}\ge e^{-\Sigma_z},
\]

and hence

\[
a(x)\ge a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the upper chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(z)\), then \(U\le a(x)\), so the lower chain also accepts. Thus the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur.

Hence in all cases,

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z\implies \mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
}
\]

---

## (5) Coalescence from extremal states

Let

\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]

For a fixed realization of \(f_1,\dots,f_t\), define

\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

Each \(f_i\) is monotone by part (4), so \(F\) is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then certainly

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

For any \(x\in \mathcal X\),

\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]

By monotonicity of \(F\),

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the endpoints are equal, this forces

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant. Therefore

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant } \Longleftrightarrow F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

---

### Convention for \(h\)

As written, if \(h\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), so the later claim \(h(z)\le n\) would be false. Thus the intended height is the number of strict steps in such a chain. Equivalently, it is the literal chain-size definition minus \(1\). This shift does not affect any difference \(h(Y)-h(X)\).

So in what follows, take

\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\exists x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]

where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

---

## (6) Strict order increases height by at least \(1\)

Suppose \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\). Then \(x_t\prec y_t\).

Let

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t
\]

be a maximal chain ending at \(x_t\). Appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]

Therefore there is a chain of length \(h(x_t)+1\) ending at \(y_t\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
}
\]

---

## (7) Tail bound using the height difference

Define

\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]

By monotonicity,

\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]

for every \(t\). Also, once \(X_t=Y_t\), the two trajectories remain equal forever because they are driven by the same future maps. Therefore

\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]

On \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives

\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}
=
\mathbf 1_{\{X_t\neq Y_t\}}
\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]

Taking expectations,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le \mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
}
\]

---

## (8) Bounding the height and its expectation

Let

\[
r(z):=\#\{v\in V:z_v=1\}.
\]

If \(a\prec b\), then \(r(b)>r(a)\). Hence along any strict chain ending at \(z\), the value of \(r\) increases by at least \(1\) at every step, and the final value is \(r(z)\). Therefore

\[
h(z)\le r(z).
\]

Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), flip the \(r(z)\) sites where \(z_v=1\) one at a time. This gives a strict chain of length \(r(z)\) ending at \(z\). Hence

\[
h(z)=r(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
0\le h(z)\le |V|=n.
}
\]

Now let

\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]

Then \(X_t\sim \mu_t\) and \(Y_t\sim \nu_t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h).
\]

Since \(0\le h\le n\), the function \(h/n\) is \([0,1]\)-valued. Therefore, by the variational characterization of total variation distance,

\[
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h)
\le
n\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]

If

\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

then

\[
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le \bar d(t).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

Combining with part (7),

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\)

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Let

\[
d(t):=\max_x \|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

and define

\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard facts:

1. \(d(t)\le \bar d(t)\le 2d(t)\).
2. \(\bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t)\) for all \(s,t\ge 0\).
3. Therefore
   \[
   \bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le 2d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le \frac12.
   \]

Hence, for every integer \(m\ge 1\),

\[
\bar d(m t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
\bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})^m
\le
2^{-m}.
\]

Take \(m=k+L\). By part (8),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
|V|\,\bar d((k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}}).
\]

Since \(|V|=2L\),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}.
\]

For integer \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore

\[
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(T>t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k+L)\bigr)\le \frac1{2^k}.
}
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

First note the elementary tail lemma: if \(U\ge 0\) and

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)\le 2^{-k}
\]

for all integers \(k\ge 0\), then

\[
\mathbb E[U]
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(U>s)\,ds
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(U>k)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}
=
2.
\]

Now let \(m=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\), and define

\[
U:=\left(\frac{T}{m}-L\right)_+.
\]

Then for every integer \(k\ge 0\),

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)
=
\mathbb P\left(T>m(k+L)\right)
\le
2^{-k}
\]

by part (9). Hence \(\mathbb E[U]\le 2\).

Since

\[
\frac{T}{m}\le L+U,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
m(L+\mathbb E[U])
\le
m(L+2).
\]

Because \(L>1\) is an integer, \(L\ge 2\), so \(L+2\le 2L\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.
}
\]

Thus the desired bound holds with the absolute constant \(c=2\).

Let \(n=|V|\), and write \(x_v=x(v)\). Also write  
\[
D(x,z):=\{v\in V:x_v\neq z_v\}.
\]

---

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]

Thus, for \(z\neq x\),

\[
\boxed{
P(x,z)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}, & |D(x,z)|=1,\\[1.2ex]
0, & |D(x,z)|\ge 2.
\end{cases}}
\]

Equivalently, if \(D(x,z)=\{v\}\),

\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\exp\left(\frac12(z_v-x_v)\sum_{w\sim v}x_w\right)\right\}.
\]

---

Let \(Z=\sum_y e^{-H(y)}\), so \(\pi(x)=Z^{-1}e^{-H(x)}\).

We prove detailed balance. If \(x,z\) differ at more than one coordinate, then \(P(x,z)=P(z,x)=0\). If \(x,z\) differ at exactly one coordinate, then by part (1),

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]

The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\), so

\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]

The equality is trivial for \(x=z\). Hence the chain is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). Therefore, by the detailed balance theorem,

\[
\sum_x \pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\sum_x \pi(z)P(z,x)
=
\pi(z)\sum_x P(z,x)
=
\pi(z).
\]

So \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}
\Big[(1-Sx_t(w))-(1-x_t(v)x_t(w))\Big].
\]

Simplifying,

\[
H(y)-H(x_t)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(x_t(v)-S)x_t(w).
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
e^{-(H(y)-H(x_t))}
=
\exp\left(
\frac12\sum_{w\in N_v}(S-x_t(v))x_t(w)
\right).
\]

So

\[
\boxed{
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1}-x_t(v_{t+1}))x_t(w)\right).
}
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

Fix a realization of \((v_{t+1},S_{t+1},U_{t+1})\). We show that if \(x\preceq z\), then

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_w=x_w\le z_w=f_{t+1}(z)_w.
\]

Thus we only need to check the chosen vertex \(v=v_{t+1}\).

\[
\Sigma_\eta:=\sum_{w\sim v}\eta_w
\]

for a configuration \(\eta\).

If \(z_v=+1\), then \(f_{t+1}(z)_v=+1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le +1=f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(z_v=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(x_v=-1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(-1\) to \(+1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), we have \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
a(x)\le a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the lower chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(x)\), then necessarily \(U\le a(z)\), so the upper chain also accepts. Hence the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur. Therefore

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

### Case 2: \(S_{t+1}=-1\)

If \(x_v=-1\), then \(f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\), so automatically

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=-1\le f_{t+1}(z)_v.
\]

The only nontrivial case is \(x_v=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), we also have \(z_v=+1\). Thus both chains propose changing \(+1\) to \(-1\).

By part (3), the acceptance probability from configuration \(\eta\) is

\[
a(\eta)=\min\{1,e^{-\Sigma_\eta}\}.
\]

Since \(x\preceq z\), \(\Sigma_x\le \Sigma_z\), so

\[
e^{-\Sigma_x}\ge e^{-\Sigma_z},
\]

and hence

\[
a(x)\ge a(z).
\]

Therefore, if the upper chain accepts, i.e. if \(U\le a(z)\), then \(U\le a(x)\), so the lower chain also accepts. Thus the bad event

\[
f_{t+1}(x)_v=+1,\qquad f_{t+1}(z)_v=-1
\]

cannot occur.

Hence in all cases,

\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
x\preceq z\implies \mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
}
\]

---

## (5) Coalescence from extremal states

Let

\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]

For a fixed realization of \(f_1,\dots,f_t\), define

\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1.
\]

Each \(f_i\) is monotone by part (4), so \(F\) is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then certainly

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose

\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

For any \(x\in \mathcal X\),

\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]

By monotonicity of \(F\),

\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]

Since the endpoints are equal, this forces

\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Thus \(F\) is constant. Therefore

\[
\boxed{
F \text{ is constant } \Longleftrightarrow F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
}
\]

---

### Convention for \(h\)

As written, if \(h\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), so the later claim \(h(z)\le n\) would be false. Thus the intended height is the number of strict steps in such a chain. Equivalently, it is the literal chain-size definition minus \(1\). This shift does not affect any difference \(h(Y)-h(X)\).

So in what follows, take

\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\exists x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]

where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

---

## (6) Strict order increases height by at least \(1\)

Suppose \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\). Then \(x_t\prec y_t\).

Let

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t
\]

be a maximal chain ending at \(x_t\). Appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain

\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]

Therefore there is a chain of length \(h(x_t)+1\) ending at \(y_t\). Hence

\[
\boxed{
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
}
\]

---

## (7) Tail bound using the height difference

Define

\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]

By monotonicity,

\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]

for every \(t\). Also, once \(X_t=Y_t\), the two trajectories remain equal forever because they are driven by the same future maps. Therefore

\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]

On \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives

\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}
=
\mathbf 1_{\{X_t\neq Y_t\}}
\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]

Taking expectations,

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le \mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
}
\]

---

## (8) Bounding the height and its expectation

Let

\[
r(z):=\#\{v\in V:z_v=1\}.
\]

If \(a\prec b\), then \(r(b)>r(a)\). Hence along any strict chain ending at \(z\), the value of \(r\) increases by at least \(1\) at every step, and the final value is \(r(z)\). Therefore

\[
h(z)\le r(z).
\]

Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), flip the \(r(z)\) sites where \(z_v=1\) one at a time. This gives a strict chain of length \(r(z)\) ending at \(z\). Hence

\[
h(z)=r(z).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
0\le h(z)\le |V|=n.
}
\]

Now let

\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]

Then \(X_t\sim \mu_t\) and \(Y_t\sim \nu_t\). Hence

\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h).
\]

Since \(0\le h\le n\), the function \(h/n\) is \([0,1]\)-valued. Therefore, by the variational characterization of total variation distance,

\[
\nu_t(h)-\mu_t(h)
\le
n\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]

If

\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

then

\[
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le \bar d(t).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

Combining with part (7),

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(T>t)\le |V|\,\bar d(t).
}
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}\)

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Let

\[
d(t):=\max_x \|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]

and define

\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard facts:

1. \(d(t)\le \bar d(t)\le 2d(t)\).
2. \(\bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t)\) for all \(s,t\ge 0\).
3. Therefore
   \[
   \bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le 2d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})
   \le \frac12.
   \]

Hence, for every integer \(m\ge 1\),

\[
\bar d(m t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
\bar d(t_{\mathrm{mix}})^m
\le
2^{-m}.
\]

Take \(m=k+L\). By part (8),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
|V|\,\bar d((k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}}).
\]

Since \(|V|=2L\),

\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}.
\]

For integer \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore

\[
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P\bigl(T>t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k+L)\bigr)\le \frac1{2^k}.
}
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

First note the elementary tail lemma: if \(U\ge 0\) and

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)\le 2^{-k}
\]

for all integers \(k\ge 0\), then

\[
\mathbb E[U]
=
\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(U>s)\,ds
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(U>k)
\le
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}
=
2.
\]

Now let \(m=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\), and define

\[
U:=\left(\frac{T}{m}-L\right)_+.
\]

Then for every integer \(k\ge 0\),

\[
\mathbb P(U>k)
=
\mathbb P\left(T>m(k+L)\right)
\le
2^{-k}
\]

by part (9). Hence \(\mathbb E[U]\le 2\).

Since

\[
\frac{T}{m}\le L+U,
\]

we get

\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
m(L+\mathbb E[U])
\le
m(L+2).
\]

Because \(L>1\) is an integer, \(L\ge 2\), so \(L+2\le 2L\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.
}
\]

Thus the desired bound holds with the absolute constant \(c=2\).
